Europe’s space industry is heating up, and it’s starting to attract outside attention.
CUBECOM, the South African company developing RF communications systems for satellites, today announced it’s opening a new office in Delft, the Netherlands as part of an effort to lock down more deals across the continent.
The new office will initially host the company’s sales and customer team, with the goal of forming stronger relationships with clients in the region, but will eventually include technical staff and engineers to develop European IP. CUBECOM ultimately aims to establish a regional production facility within the next five years.
Good hopes: The move comes in response to an explosive increase in demand from European customers, which represent over half of the company’s yearly revenue, according to CEO Sampie Booysen. In 2026, CUBECOM sold 300+ components to European customers, driving a 3x growth in revenue compared to last year. By moving to Delft, CUBECOM is trying to keep up the momentum.
“Europe has increased their defense and space budgets significantly, and we see that there is a big push for individual countries to have their own sovereign capabilities,” Booysen said. “A couple of years back, you’d do two or three units at a time, and all of a sudden, the volume has just quadrupled. So, [now] you’re selling tens or twenties of a subsystem.”
CUBECOM is targeting €30M ($32.9M) in revenues by 2030 or 2031, according to Booysen, which would represent a sixfold increase in its revenues today. Much of that projection is built on successfully establishing a presence in the European market.
Table (Mountain) stakes: CUBECOM’s ability to deliver on these increasingly large contracts has been due, in large part, to upgrading its production capacity in South Africa. That investment helped double CUBECOM’s workforce, and allowed the company to produce new comms equipment including Ka-band, S-band, and X-band antennas and transmitters.
But as European buyers become more concerned with building sovereign systems using only European-made components, CUBECOM’s new office in Delft aims to ensure that it doesn’t lose future deals due to distance.
“If we compare Asia and the US to Europe, Europe is actually a much harder market segment to penetrate because it’s so geopolitical,” CUBECOM Chief Growth Officer Mariechen Du Plessis told Payload. “Even though we’re a commercial entity selling commercial products to commercial missions most of the time, there are also a lot of challenges around sovereignty…so to us it’s exciting to be part of that conversation.”
Inflection Space System’s first mission, Pax, will launch NET 2028 on a rideshare booked through Exolaunch.
Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled its new reusable reentry vehicle—called REV1—at Space Tech Expo in Bremen, Germany today.
Asynchronics today announced the closing of a $3.1M seed round to bring more affordable digital-twin software to the market, and grow its virtual catalog of off-the-shelf components.
German satellite-components manufacturer Dcubed announced the closing of a €27.2M ($30M) Series A extension round today, which comes in addition to an earlier €4.4M ($4.9M) Series A round, which closed in August 2024.
The new capital will fund an expansion of the company’s production facilities in the US and Germany with the goal of quadrupling its production rate of actuators and solar arrays. It will also pay to develop a new family of advanced solar arrays and satellite power systems—called ARAQYS.
Warsaw Equity Group led the round, which included participation from the European Innovation Council, HTGF Opportunity Fund, BayBG, and Expansion Aerospace Ventures.
